lesson.title: Power: batteries and the sun
lesson.subtitle: Make a sensor last, then keep it going on sunshine

video.title: Power: batteries and the sun
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor kneels by a dry garden bed, holding a small sensor box whose light is off; a calendar shows eight weeks crossed out.
scenes.animation: The sensor's light blinks, fades, goes dark; calendar pages flip.
scenes.narration: We left a soil sensor in the school garden over the long holiday. It sent a reading over Wi-Fi every minute, on two AA batteries. It died in under three weeks. The holiday lasted eight.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: power from batteries and the sun.

scenes.visual: Two AA batteries with '2,500 mAh' on the label; the formula writes itself beside them.
scenes.animation: The label glows; the division sign slides in.
scenes.narration: A battery's capacity is in milliamp-hours: two AA batteries hold about two thousand five hundred. Divide it by the average current, in milliamps, to get hours. And plan with seventy percent of the label.

scenes.visual: Three bars: sleeping is a sliver, measuring is short, sending towers over both.
scenes.animation: Bars grow one by one; the sending bar shoots up.
scenes.narration: Where does the power go? Asleep, a sensor draws about a hundredth of a milliamp; measuring takes about five, for a tenth of a second. But sending over Wi-Fi takes a hundred and twenty, for two whole seconds.

scenes.visual: The sum on the board beside the garden sensor, line by line.
scenes.animation: Each line writes in as it is said; '18 days' is circled.
scenes.narration: So our garden sensor, sending once a minute, averaged about four milliamps. Seventy percent of two thousand five hundred is one thousand seven hundred and fifty. Divided by four, that's about four hundred and forty hours: eighteen days.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma at the board with the garden sensor's sum. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Which change makes the batteries last longest: measuring less often, sending every fifteen minutes, or four batteries instead of two?

scenes.visual: Two clocks: one ticking every minute with a draining battery, one every fifteen minutes with a battery that barely moves.
scenes.animation: The left battery empties fast; the right one hardly changes.
scenes.narration: Send every fifteen minutes. The average drops from four milliamps to under a third of one, so the same batteries last about nine months, not eighteen days. Four batteries would only double it.

scenes.visual: The sun, a small panel on a pole, a battery box and the sensor in the soil, joined by arrows; clouds pass.
scenes.animation: Energy flows along the arrows by day; at night only the battery glows.
scenes.narration: To run all year, add a small solar panel and a rechargeable battery. The panel charges by day; the battery carries the sensor through nights and clouds. Much of Africa and the Middle East gets four to six hours of full sun a day, but plan for three to five cloudy days in a row.

scenes.visual: A worked sizing sum on the board, beside a postcard-sized panel and a battery pack.
scenes.animation: Each line writes in; the panel grows to three times a day's bar.
scenes.narration: Size it for our Wi-Fi sensor. It uses about a hundred milliamp-hours a day; five cloudy days need five hundred, or a little over seven hundred with the seventy percent rule. And the panel should make three times the daily use, to catch up after clouds.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside a sensor with a tiny panel; a weather strip shows sun, then four cloudy days. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. This battery covers five cloudy days, but the panel only just covers one day's use in full sun. Will it run all year?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a battery, a percent sign, a clock, the sun.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: No: with nothing to spare, the panel can't catch up after cloudy days. Remember: capacity divided by average current gives hours, plan with seventy percent, send less often, and give the panel room to spare.

scenes.visual: Groups at desks with sensor cards and calculators; the board has a column of answers in days.
scenes.animation: One group's answer jumps from days to months.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: battery-life sums on the board. Give each group a sensor card with a battery, a radio and how often it sends. They work out how long it lasts, then change one thing to make it last a term. Next time: getting the data home.

checkpoints.prompt: The sensor sends over Wi-Fi every minute. Which change makes its batteries last longest?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — sending is the costly part, so sending every 15 minutes cuts the average current from about 4 mA to under 0.3 mA.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — measuring is cheap, and twice the batteries only doubles the life. Sending is the costly part: send every 15 minutes.

checkpoints.prompt: The battery covers 5 cloudy days, but the panel only just covers one day's use in full sun. Will it run all year?

options.text: No: it can't catch up after clouds
Yes: the panel covers each day

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — after cloudy days the panel has nothing spare to refill the battery, so it slowly runs flat. Aim for about three times the daily use.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a panel that only just covers one day has nothing spare. After cloudy days the battery never refills, and the sensor stops.
